RDS-LOG-01.title: Debug log level: volume, information content and cost
RDS-LOG-01.subtitle: **Executed 2026-09-14.** Evidence: (evidence held internally), shared with RDS-PWR-02. A measurement case: its output is a table, not a verdict.
RDS-LOG-01.objective: Establish what each log level of the vendor daemon costs and what it buys, so that later cases can choose a level deliberately and so Mujina's own logging can be designed against a known comparison.
RDS-LOG-01.requirements: - One RDS 2.0 unit, vendor firmware, reachable over ssh. - Enough free space on `/data` for the run (200 MB minimum).
RDS-LOG-01.procedure: 1. Stop the vendor stack. 2. Start the daemon with `-L <level>`, output to a file on the unit. 3. Run through power-on; collect the log; delete it from the unit. 4. Count total lines, distinct lines, and distinct **message shapes** — lines with all digit runs replaced by `N`, so per-ASIC iteration collapses to the statement that produced it.
RDS-LOG-01.pass_fail: Pass: Not a pass/fail case. It is a measurement, and its output is the table below. Fail: Abort if `/data` free space falls below 200 MB during the run, or if the collected log is empty.
RDS-LOG-01.metrics: Named before the run, not chosen after it. Per log level, from the collected capture: total lines, bytes, distinct message shapes, and lines per new shape. From the controller, once: the daemon's option set and the level in force. The derived quantity that decides the answer is **new shapes at this level**, because it is the only one that says what a level buys rather than what it costs.
RDS-LOG-01.comments: The content is real — 78,194 distinct strings, one per ASIC per round — but the *structure* is 6,767 statements. For sequence work, `-L 6` is the right level; `-L 7` is for when the per-ASIC values themselves are the subject, and then only briefly. The daemon's log macro writes to **stdout and syslog on every call**. At `-L 7` that is 2,700 writes per second to both. See RDS-PWR-02 for what happens when stdout is a network pipe.
RDS-LOG-01.configurations: - `-L 5` notice (daemon default), `-L 6` info, `-L 7` debug. - `-b <mask>` would restrict this to one hashboard, cutting volume and power to a third — **but it is compiled out of release builds**: the option parser is inside `#ifdef DEBUG_MODE`, and a shipped daemon accepts only `-s`, `-B`, `-F` and `-L`. Its usage text lists the full set regardless, so the text cannot be trusted. Obtaining the mask means building the package with `DEBUG_MODE` defined, which we can do from the vendor build system.

RDS-LOG-02.title: Power-on log-level ladder
RDS-LOG-02.subtitle: **Executed 2026-09-14**, four rungs. Evidence: (evidence held internally), one directory per rung, with the computed comparison `LADDER.md` across them.
RDS-LOG-02.objective: Establish, for one power-on on one hashboard, what each log level costs in volume and buys in distinct information, so every later case can choose a level deliberately instead of by habit. Produce the stock baseline corpus that our own carrier work will be argued against.
RDS-LOG-02.requirements: - One RDS 2.0 unit, reachable over ssh. - The debug daemon at `/data/bin/bzmd-debug` (board mask), the installed daemon untouched. - One hashboard, board mask 1. No *external* work: no pool, no miner started. The vendor stack dispatches its own work during power-on and calibration regardless, which is why a rung costs about a kilowatt at the wall rather than a third of powered idle. - Free RAM on the unit's tmpfs above the cap plus headroom.
RDS-LOG-02.procedure: For each level in 4, 5, 6, 7, in that order: 1. Confirm no vendor daemon is running, by exact process name. 2. Launch the debug daemon on board 0 at that level, output to the unit's tmpfs, with a hard 300-second ceiling and a size cap. 3. Let power-on run without intervention. Record the verdict it reports. 4. Collect the log, stop the daemon, remove the file from the unit. 5. Settle for 60 seconds before the next rung. Then compute, per rung: lines, bytes, distinct **message shapes** (a line with digit runs and hex literals replaced by placeholders), and the count of shapes appearing at that level and no lower one.
RDS-LOG-02.pass_fail: Pass: Not pass/fail. It is a measurement, and its output is the comparison table. The run is valid if every rung either reports a power-on verdict or is recorded as silent with the daemon demonstrably alive. Fail: - Free tmpfs falls below the cap plus headroom: abort before launching. - A rung's daemon is not running eight seconds after launch: abort the ladder. - A rung exceeds the size cap: the watchdog stops that daemon, and the rung is recorded as capped rather than silently truncated.
RDS-LOG-02.metrics: Named before the run, not chosen after it. Per rung: total lines, bytes, distinct message shapes, shapes appearing at that level and no lower one, lines per new shape, and the power-on verdict. Sampled from the controller throughout: fan speed, fan duty, load average, available memory, and the capture's size on the unit. Free space on the capture target is sampled as well as the capture's own size, because the daemon writes to the system log in the same filesystem and a cap that watches only its own file is measuring the wrong thing.
RDS-LOG-02.comments: Sets the level every later vendor case runs at, and sets the standard our own log output is designed against. A level that multiplies volume without adding shapes is a level nobody should run, and we should not build one.
RDS-LOG-02.configurations: Board mask 1 of 3, no external job source, tmpfs target, 250 MB cap, 300-second ceiling per rung. Measured cost: about 1,056 W at the wall through power-on and 1,438 W through calibration, for roughly two and a half minutes per rung. Bounded and short rather than cheap; the ceiling is what bounds it.

RDS-LOG-03.title: Runtime log-level control, and what the top level is made of
RDS-LOG-03.subtitle: **Executed 2026-09-14.** Evidence: (evidence held internally). A measurement case.
RDS-LOG-03.objective: Two things at once, on one powered board: 1. Prove that the log level can be **raised and lowered while the daemon runs**, so a debug capture can be a window around a phase rather than a tax on the whole run. 2. Establish what the top level consists of **in steady state**, as opposed to during power-on, which RDS-LOG-01 already measured.
RDS-LOG-03.requirements: - One RDS 2.0 unit, reachable over ssh. - The debug daemon at `/data/bin/bzmd-debug`, built with the option set that restores the board mask and carrying the two signal handlers. Built by `tools/rds/build-debug-daemon.sh`; the installed daemon is not touched. - One hashboard only. The mask keeps this near a third of powered-idle draw.
RDS-LOG-03.procedure: 1. Start the debug daemon on board 0 at `-L 4`, output to a file on the unit. 2. Let power-on complete without intervention. 3. Raise the level three times, one step each, pausing between steps, and record the file size after each. 4. Lower it twice and record the growth over the following seconds. 5. Collect the log, stop the daemon, remove the file from the unit.
RDS-LOG-03.pass_fail: Pass: - Each raise increases the level by exactly one and the effect is visible in output volume. - Each lower decreases it, and the top-level firehose stops. - The daemon survives every signal and continues its normal work. Fail: - The daemon dies, faults, or loses the chain on any signal. - A level change has no effect, or changes by more than one step.
RDS-LOG-03.metrics: Named before the run, not chosen after it. Bytes written to the capture after each level change, at a fixed interval. Per-device telemetry for the whole window: device id, thermal reading, both voltage sense points. Wall-clock time of each signal. The derived quantities are bytes per second at each level, and the count of distinct devices reporting — the second is what turns a volume measurement into a statement about coverage.
RDS-LOG-03.comments: The board reported 100 ASICs and 23,600 engines at power-on, and 23,600 is exactly 100 × 236. The exactness suggests a nominal figure rather than a discovered count, so it is evidence about what the vendor stack assumes, not proof of what the silicon contains. Recorded against the engine-count question in epic #14 and raised as a gap in the hardware reference. No raw wire bytes appear anywhere in this capture at any level. Replay in the sense of #56 therefore cannot be built from vendor logs; it needs either a tap on the link or recording from inside our own driver. That settles the open question in #56.

RDS-PWR-01.title: Power-on sequence: PSU ramp, MCU enables, board verdict
RDS-PWR-01.subtitle: **Executed 2026-09-15.** Evidence: (evidence held internally). The first attempt, on 2026-09-14, ran under the defective capture method that RDS-PWR-02 documents, so it recorded the sequence and not a verdict. It did not need a dedicated re-run in the end: the corrected harness captured a complete p
RDS-PWR-01.objective: Record the vendor daemon's complete power-on sequence — every PSU command, MCU enable, trip-protection write and round — with values, so Mujina's own bring-up (#28, #29) can be written against an observed sequence rather than an inferred one.
RDS-PWR-01.requirements: - One RDS 2.0 unit, vendor firmware, boards unpowered. - `tools/rds/rds-testcase.sh` with its default tmpfs target and watchdog.
RDS-PWR-01.procedure: 1. `tools/rds/rds-testcase.sh <unit> RDS-PWR-01 6 0` 2. The harness stops the vendor stack, launches the daemon detached on the unit at `-L 6`, polls with one-shot connections, and collects. 3. `RESULT.md` is computed from the log: sequence markers with line numbers, PSU voltage steps, rounds reached, and volume by message shape.
RDS-PWR-01.pass_fail: Pass: `system power on done`, and every marker in the expected sequence present in order: PSU init, per-board MCU engine-power and oscillator enables, PSU enable, trip-protection programming, the voltage ramp, and the round progression to a verdict. Fail: Any of: `system power on fail`; the daemon exiting; a marker absent from the sequence; or the PSU commanded outside 12,000–19,000 mV. Executable, abort.
RDS-PWR-01.metrics: Named before the run, not chosen after it. The commanded and measured rail voltage and the supply current at every step of the ramp, with a timestamp for each. Board inlet and outlet temperatures, control-board temperature, fan duty and speed, sampled from the controller throughout. The power-on verdict and its elapsed time.
RDS-PWR-01.comments: The trip protection being programmed **before** the ramp is the ordering that matters: the hardware backstop is armed before the voltage climbs. The plan's safety rule ("set the MCU's trip protection at bring-up") is confirmed as what the vendor actually does, and now has values.

RDS-PWR-02.title: Power-on under logging back-pressure
RDS-PWR-02.subtitle: **Executed 2026-09-14.** Evidence: (evidence held internally). The failure is the finding; the verdict is computed from the evidence. Evidence: (evidence held internally), `daemon.log` 244,988 lines / 24 MB, sha256 `4097fc0932c5e1d6…`.
RDS-PWR-02.objective: Determine whether debug-level logging is safe to run through the whole power-on sequence, and if not, why not. Unplanned: this case exists because a characterization run at `-L 7` failed to power the boards on, and the failure turned out to be more informative than the capture would have been.
RDS-PWR-02.requirements: One RDS 2.0 unit, vendor firmware, boards powered down and idle.
RDS-PWR-02.procedure: 1. Stop the vendor stack so the boards are unpowered. 2. Start the daemon with `-L 7`, **stdout piped over ssh to the controller** (this is the condition under test, and it is the wrong way to do it). 3. Observe the power-on sequence to its verdict.
RDS-PWR-02.pass_fail: Pass: `system power on done` within the daemon's own round budget, with the boards reaching their target and the daemon proceeding to calibration. Fail: `system power on fail`, or the daemon exiting. **Executable, and it aborts the case.**
RDS-PWR-02.metrics: Named before the run, not chosen after it. Everything RDS-PWR-01 captures, plus the quantity this case exists to observe: where the capture stalls relative to the daemon's own timestamps. The gap between a log line's stated time and its arrival is the measurement.
RDS-PWR-02.comments: 1. **Logging must never be able to change what it observes.** Mujina's tracing is asynchronous and non-blocking by default, which is the right property; this case is the argument for never introducing a synchronous logging path on a timed sequence, and for treating that as a correctness property rather than a performance one. 2. **A bounded, droppable channel beats a complete one.** When a debug stream cannot keep up, the right failure is dropped lines with a counter, not a stalled producer. Worth stating explicitly wherever Mujina gains a high-rate diagnostic channel (#44). 3. **Capture design for the measurement harness (#26):** write to the unit's RAM, cap it, collect afterwards. `tools/rds/rds-testcase.sh` now does this by default and carries a watchdog that stops the capture on size or on a requested window. 4. **The ramp is now specified.** The PSU steps 16.5 V to 19.0 V in 500 mV increments while the MCU enables engine and oscillator power per board, with trip protection set to 115 °C and 500 mV per channel beforehand. That is a sequence Mujina must reproduce for #28 and #29, and these are the numbers to reproduce it with.
RDS-PWR-02.configurations: | | | |---|---| | failing | `-L 7`, stdout through ssh to the controller | | corrected | `-L 7`, stdout to a file on the unit's **tmpfs**, collected after, with a size cap and a window | | routine | `-L 6`, which removes every high-volume shape (RDS-LOG-01) | The level **cannot be changed while the daemon runs**: `-L` is read once at startup and nothing writes it afterwards, and only SIGTERM is handled. So a debug capture is bounded by the lifetime of the run, and short, targeted runs are the only windowing the stock binary allows.

RDS-CAL-01.title: Calibration and plug-and-play: search, convergence, persistence
RDS-CAL-01.subtitle: ** not executed.**
RDS-CAL-01.objective: Observe how the vendor stack searches for an operating point: what it varies, in what order, what it measures to decide, how long it takes, what it writes to persistent storage, and what it does with a board that will not converge.
RDS-CAL-01.requirements: - One RDS 2.0 unit, one hashboard, boards powered by the vendor path. - A capture of the persistent areas **before** the run, so what calibration writes can be established by difference rather than by assumption. - Log level 6, with a window at the top level opened around the search itself using the runtime signal (RDS-LOG-03).
RDS-CAL-01.procedure: 1. Capture the persistent areas and hash them. 2. Start the debug daemon on one board with calibration enabled, at level 6. 3. When power-on reports done, raise to the top level for the search, and lower it again once the search concludes. 4. Let the search run to its own conclusion. Do not intervene. 5. Capture the persistent areas again and diff against step 1. 6. Repeat the whole case once on the same board, from the stored result, to observe what a second boot does differently.
RDS-CAL-01.pass_fail: Pass: - The search terminates on its own and reports a converged operating point. - The difference in persistent storage is fully accounted for: every changed file is either explained or recorded as unexplained, by name. - The second run reuses the stored result rather than searching again, or the case records that it does not. Fail: - The search does not terminate within the case window. - A board is left in a state that fails to power on subsequently. This is the one case in this suite that writes to persistent storage, so recovery is checked before it runs, not after it fails.
RDS-CAL-01.metrics: Named before the run, not chosen after it. Before and after: a hash of every file in the persistent areas, so what calibration writes is established by difference rather than assumption. During: the search trajectory — each operating point tried, with voltage, frequency, pass rate and throughput — and elapsed time to convergence. At the end: the stored result, and on the second run whether it was reused or re-derived.
RDS-CAL-01.comments: The specification for #9, which proposes a different calibration objective (marginal efficiency rather than pass rate). We cannot argue for a better objective without the incumbent's behaviour measured. Also supplies the operating-point table shape for #7 and the search trajectory the chain model in #57 must be able to reproduce.
RDS-CAL-01.configurations: One board. Calibration enabled. Frequency and voltage left at their defaults so the search is the vendor's own, not one we steered.

RDS-ENG-01.title: Engine enumeration: nominal population versus discovered
RDS-ENG-01.subtitle: ** not executed.** Partially anticipated by RDS-LOG-03, which is why the objective below is narrower than it once was.
RDS-ENG-01.objective: Settle the engine-count question that every hit-rate denominator and every nonce-range partition depends on, and settle it in the right terms. RDS-LOG-03 already observed the vendor stack reporting 100 devices and 23,600 engines for one board — exactly 100 × 236. The exactness is the finding: it argues a **nominal** figure the firmware assumes rather than a count it discovered. So the open question is no longer "236 or 512" but: **Settled 2026-09-15, and not by this case.** The public integration guide states it outright: 236 hashing engine tiles per ASIC, 4 engines per tile, 944 engines total, with the ×4 carried inside its own throughput estimate. Our measured 23,600 across 100 devices is 100 × 236, so the vendor stack counts **tiles**. There was never a conflict between 236 and 944; I built an argument between a tile count and a core count that were printed side by side. The 512 figure that appeared in a requirements document is a **third** claim and is supported by no source either of us can find. It needs its own provenance rather than being treated as the alternative to 236.
RDS-ENG-01.requirements: - One RDS 2.0 unit with a powered, calibrated board. - A way to address engine positions individually and observe whether each answers — from Mujina's diagnostic surface, not the vendor stack, since the vendor stack is the source of the nominal figure under test.
RDS-ENG-01.procedure: 1. Bring one board to powered and calibrated by the vendor path. 2. Hand over to Mujina without dropping board power. 3. Read a known register at each engine position across the whole addressable range, including positions above the nominal count and inside the non-engine region the protocol reference describes. 4. Record, per device, which positions answered, which did not, and which returned something unexpected.
RDS-ENG-01.pass_fail: Pass: Not pass/fail. The output is a population map per device. The case is valid if every device on the board was probed and the result is reproducible across two consecutive runs. Fail: - Probing disturbs the chain such that the board loses calibration or power. - The two runs disagree about which positions answer. Disagreement is not noise here; it means the probe method is unsound and the map is worthless.
RDS-ENG-01.metrics: Named before the run, not chosen after it. Per device: which engine positions answered, which did not, and which returned something unexpected. Two consecutive runs of the same probe, so reproducibility is measured rather than assumed. Separately and explicitly: the count of addressable positions and the hashing capacity, so the ratio between them can be asserted rather than inferred.
RDS-ENG-01.comments: The protocol reference explicitly warns that engine IDs may have holes and must not be assumed contiguous. A map with holes is therefore an expected outcome, not an anomaly, and the case is written to record it rather than to confirm a round number.

RDS-THR-01.title: Thermal response and fan control at powered idle
RDS-THR-01.subtitle: **Executed 2026-09-15**, arm A. Evidence: (evidence held internally). Arm B, which moves the setpoint, is not yet run. Verdict is computed from the evidence and shown on the matrix, not restated here.
RDS-THR-01.objective: Observe the **closed loop**, not the endpoints: how fan duty tracks die temperature once the controller is actually running. Rewritten 2026-09-15. The first version asked for "the fan curve at powered idle" and would have measured the wrong thing, because the loop does not start until calibration completes, then waits about 180 seconds to settle and averages several samples before its first move. A run that ends before that sees a constant duty and concludes there is no feedback. One did, and it was reported as a finding before Ronald corrected it. See `docs/rds/fan-control-law.md`.
RDS-THR-01.requirements: - One RDS 2.0 unit, one hashboard powered, no jobs. - Fan and temperature readings sampled from the controller, not from inside the daemon's log, so the two are independent records of the same thing.
RDS-THR-01.procedure: 1. Power one board by the vendor path at log level 6. 2. Sample fan speed, duty and every available temperature at a fixed interval for the whole run, from the controller. 3. **Hold for at least 30 minutes after calibration completes.** Not a margin picked for comfort: it is the settle wait plus enough sample windows to see several adjustments. Anything shorter measures the feed-forward startup value and reports it as the control law. 3. Open a top-level window long enough to capture one full per-device telemetry sweep, then lower it again. 4. Record the spread of die temperature across devices, not only the extremes: RDS-LOG-03 observed a 12-degree spread at a uniform commanded frequency.
RDS-THR-01.pass_fail: Pass: - Fan duty is a reproducible function of the temperature the daemon reads. - The controller's independent samples agree with the daemon's own readings within a stated tolerance. Disagreement is a finding about which one to trust, and is worth more than agreement. Fail: - Any device exceeds its thermal limit at idle. That is a hardware fault and the case aborts rather than continuing to observe it. - Fan control does not respond at all, which would mean the curve is not being driven by the quantity assumed.
RDS-THR-01.metrics: Named before the run, not chosen after it. From the daemon: every control-loop report — elapsed time, average die temperature, target, duty and fan speed — and the spread across devices, not only the extremes. From the controller, independently and at a fixed interval: fan speed, duty, and every available temperature. Both sides are captured on purpose. Where the two disagree, that disagreement is a finding about which one to trust and is worth more than agreement.
RDS-THR-01.comments: Direct input to #45 (fan control) and #8 (self-characterised thermal resistance). The idle spread across devices is the quiescent term that any per-device thermal model needs before load is added, and it feeds the thermal coupling in #57.

MJ-BAUD-01.title: 5 Mbaud on the vendor 9-bit tty driver
MJ-BAUD-01.subtitle: **Executed 2026-09-14.** Evidence: (evidence held internally). Runs before MJ-DIAG-01, deliberately. Verdict is computed from the evidence.
MJ-BAUD-01.objective: Establish whether the vendor tty driver accepts the baud rate Mujina asks for by the method Mujina uses to ask. Not whether 5 Mbaud works — the vendor stack proves that nightly — but whether *our* request is honoured, silently ignored, or rejected.
MJ-BAUD-01.requirements: - One RDS 2.0 unit. **The chain need not be powered**, which is what makes this the cheapest case in the phase: it is about the driver, not the silicon. - Mujina able to open the tty, which means the vendor daemon must not hold it.
MJ-BAUD-01.procedure: 1. Stop the vendor stack so the ttys are free. Confirm by open file descriptors, not by assumption. 2. Have Mujina open the tty and set the rate the way it does in production. 3. Read the rate back **from the driver**, not from Mujina's own record of what it asked for. 4. Compare against what the vendor stack configures, read the same way. 5. Repeat for each of the three ttys: a driver that honours one and not another is a real possibility and a miserable thing to discover later.
MJ-BAUD-01.pass_fail: Pass: - The rate read back from the driver equals the rate requested, on all three ttys. - It matches what the vendor stack sets. Fail: - The rate read back differs from the rate requested, in either direction. - The request errors. - The three ttys disagree. Any of these blocks MJ-DIAG-01 rather than merely being recorded: a diagnostic run over a misconfigured link measures the misconfiguration.
MJ-BAUD-01.metrics: Named before the run, not chosen after it. Per tty: the rate requested, and the rate read back from the port after configuring it. The driver's own record of what it was asked for, as context. The read-back is the measurement. Asking the requester what it requested answers a different question.
MJ-BAUD-01.comments: The kernel log shows the driver being configured through the high-rate flags during a normal vendor start, so the capability is present. The question is purely whether our path reaches it. Tracks #23.

MJ-OBS-01.title: Mujina in observer mode against real boards
MJ-OBS-01.subtitle: **Executed 2026-09-15**, four handover windows. Evidence: (evidence held internally) is the clean one. Verdict is computed from the evidence; the analysis is in `MJ-OBS-01-result.md`.
MJ-OBS-01.objective: The first time our own code touches real silicon. Mujina attaches to the chain, enumerates it, and streams telemetry, while dispatching no work at all.
MJ-OBS-01.requirements: - One RDS 2.0 unit, one hashboard, brought to powered by the vendor path. - Mujina at `/data/mujina/mujina-minerd` with `MUJINA_OBSERVE` set, so no job source is created and the scheduler starts paused. Both, not either: a paused scheduler with a job source is one API call away from dispatching. - The handover, which kills the vendor daemon rather than stopping it: its clean stop powers the device off.
MJ-OBS-01.procedure: 1. Bring one board up by the vendor path. Confirm power-on done. 2. Start Mujina in observer mode alongside, touching no hashboard, and confirm it is healthy on its API. 3. Hand over. Record the timestamp of the last heartbeat. 4. For the whole window: read the chain summary, the enumeration and the telemetry through Mujina's API, and record every per-device voltage and thermal reading it returns. 5. Let the window close on its own. Do not extend it. 6. Restore the unit to the vendor stack and confirm it comes back.
MJ-OBS-01.pass_fail: Pass: - Mujina attaches and enumerates the chain without an error. - The device count and ids it reports match the vendor stack's: 100 devices, ids 0–99, no holes. - Telemetry values are within the range the vendor stack reported under comparable conditions. - **No work is dispatched.** Checked by the absence of dispatch in Mujina's own accounting, not by inference from throughput. - The unit returns to the vendor stack afterwards and powers on normally. Fail: - Mujina dispatches any work. Aborts immediately. - The chain does not enumerate, or enumerates differently on two consecutive attempts. - The unit does not return to a working vendor stack. This is the one that ends the night rather than the case.
MJ-OBS-01.metrics: Named before the run, not chosen after it. Elapsed time from handover to the board being registered, and to each probe answering. Per probe: bytes returned and whether they parse. From the chain: device count and ids, engine population, per-device thermal and voltage. Time is captured per step because the window is bounded and a step that is slow is as disqualifying as one that fails.
MJ-OBS-01.comments: Everything downstream. Until this passes, every claim about the BZM2 driver rests on a pseudo-terminal. It also produces the first per-device telemetry our own code has ever read, which is the cross-check against the vendor's numbers that MJ-ENUM-01 formalises.

MJ-DIAG-01.title: The diagnostic surface, in order of increasing risk
MJ-DIAG-01.subtitle: **Not executed.** Needs a handover window. MJ-BAUD-01 has since passed, so the link rate it depended on is established.
MJ-DIAG-01.objective: Exercise each read-only diagnostic against a real chain, in a fixed order that escalates from touching nothing to touching everything, so that a failure is attributable to one step rather than to the set.
MJ-DIAG-01.requirements: - MJ-BAUD-01 passed. A diagnostic over a misconfigured link measures the link. - MJ-OBS-01 passed, so attachment and enumeration are known good. - One powered board and a handover window.
MJ-DIAG-01.procedure: Run the six in order. Record the request, the response and the elapsed time for each. Stop at the first failure and record it as the case's verdict; do not continue to gather more data, because everything after it is suspect.
MJ-DIAG-01.pass_fail: Pass: - Each step returns a well-formed response within its stated time. - Suspend and resume of the telemetry stream both take effect, observably, rather than returning success and doing nothing. This is checked against the device's own state, not against our return value — the defect being guarded against returned success the whole time it was broken. Fail: - Any step returns malformed data, times out, or leaves the chain unable to answer the next step. - The chain requires a power cycle to recover. That is a defect against the diagnostic, not an inconvenience.
MJ-DIAG-01.metrics: Named before the run, not chosen after it. Per diagnostic, in order: the request, the response, and the elapsed time. Whether the telemetry stream's state actually changed on suspend and resume, read from the device rather than from our return value.
MJ-DIAG-01.comments: This is the surface #13 and #26 build on, and the first hardware confirmation that the stream-suspend fix is real rather than merely correct-looking.

MJ-ENUM-01.title: Our enumeration against the vendor's
MJ-ENUM-01.subtitle: **Not executed.** Needs a handover window, and needs MJ-OBS-01 to pass rather than merely to have run.
MJ-ENUM-01.objective: Compare what Mujina sees on the chain against what the vendor stack sees on the same chain, in the same session, and treat every disagreement as a defect in one of them until it is attributed.
MJ-ENUM-01.requirements: - One board, powered by the vendor path, and a capture of the vendor stack's own view taken in the same session — not a remembered figure from another night and another ambient. - Mujina in observer mode with the same board.
MJ-ENUM-01.procedure: 1. Capture the vendor stack's view: device count and ids, engine population, per-device thermal and voltage sense. RDS-LOG-02 shows the level to run at and RDS-LOG-03 shows how to open a window for the per-device stream. 2. Hand over. 3. Capture Mujina's view of the same quantities. 4. Compare, field by field. Record agreements as well as disagreements: an agreement across 100 devices is evidence, not a formality.
MJ-ENUM-01.pass_fail: Pass: - Device count and ids match exactly: 100 devices, ids 0–99, no holes. - Engine population matches, or the difference is explained by RDS-ENG-01's distinction between the nominal figure the vendor assumes and the positions that actually answer. - Per-device thermal and voltage readings agree within a stated tolerance, with the tolerance justified by the time between the two captures and the thermal drift observed across it, not chosen to make the numbers pass. Fail: - A device present to one observer and absent to the other. - Readings that disagree beyond tolerance on any device. - Either observer's view changing between two consecutive reads under stable conditions.
MJ-ENUM-01.metrics: Named before the run, not chosen after it. The same quantities from both observers, captured minutes apart on one board: device count and ids, engine population, per-device thermal and voltage sense. The elapsed time between the two captures, and the thermal drift across it, because the tolerance has to be argued from that rather than chosen.
MJ-ENUM-01.comments: The two captures are minutes apart on a board whose temperature is moving, so some disagreement is expected and the tolerance has to be argued rather than assumed. Where the two disagree and the cause cannot be attributed, the vendor's view is treated as correct and the difference is filed against our driver — not because it is more likely right, but because assuming the opposite hides our own defects.

RDS-MIN-01.title: Steady-state hashing: dispatch, results, telemetry cadence
RDS-MIN-01.subtitle: ** not executed. GATED** — this case dispatches work. The unit drew 3,248 W mining against 339 W powered-idle, so it needs an explicit go-ahead and a cool day.
RDS-MIN-01.objective: Observe the job path as the vendor drives it at its own operating point: dispatch cadence, how results come back, how telemetry interleaves with work, and what the steady state costs in watts per unit of work.
RDS-MIN-01.requirements: - One RDS 2.0 unit, hashboards powered and calibrated. - A stated go-ahead for the thermal load, recorded in the case run. - Log level 6 for the body of the run. The top level only in short windows, because at steady state it is 99.6% one repeated message (RDS-LOG-03) and the useful part of it is telemetry, not narrative. - Metered power for the whole run, since the objective nobody optimises is the one that needs measuring (#5).
RDS-MIN-01.procedure: 1. Bring the boards up by the vendor path and let calibration settle. 2. Start work. Hold steady state for a stated number of minutes. 3. Open a top-level window of a few seconds at steady state, and a second one later in the run, so the two can be compared for drift. 4. Record throughput, accepted work, power and die temperatures throughout. 5. Stop work before stopping the daemon, so the shutdown path is observed separately from the load being removed.
RDS-MIN-01.pass_fail: Pass: Not pass/fail against the vendor. It is the baseline the comparison case (MJ-CMP-01) is scored against. The run is valid if steady state was held for the stated duration without a board dropping out, and if power was metered continuously. Fail: - Any board drops out or trips during the run. - Metering gaps. A throughput number without the power that produced it is not a baseline, and the run is discarded rather than reported with a hole.
RDS-MIN-01.metrics: Named before the run, not chosen after it. Throughout: metered wall power, continuously and without gaps. Submitted shares with their difficulty. Reported throughput. Die temperature per device, inlet and outlet, fan duty and speed. Derived: joules per submitted share, and joules per unit of reported throughput, each stated at both the rail and the wall. A figure without its measurement boundary is not comparable to anything.
RDS-MIN-01.comments: The reference numbers every later comparison uses, and the observed dispatch cadence the chain model in #57 must reproduce before any control claim built on it means anything.
RDS-MIN-01.configurations: All boards, vendor operating point, vendor strategy. Nothing is tuned: the point is what the shipped stack does unaided.

RDS-FLU-01.title: Job flush: what a new template does to work in flight
RDS-FLU-01.subtitle: ** not executed. GATED** — dispatches work; see RDS-MIN-01.
RDS-FLU-01.objective: Observe what happens to work already in flight when a new template arrives: whether it is abandoned or allowed to finish, how the transition is sequenced across devices, how long it takes, and what fraction of work is lost. This is the path with the most opportunity to be subtly wrong in our own implementation, because everything about it looks fine when it is broken — the miner keeps hashing, and only the stale share rate tells you.
RDS-FLU-01.requirements: - One RDS 2.0 unit hashing steadily (RDS-MIN-01 conditions). - The ability to force a template change at a chosen moment. - A top-level window opened immediately before the flush and closed after it, using the runtime signal. The flush is seconds long; paying debug volume for the whole run to catch it is exactly what the signal exists to avoid.
RDS-FLU-01.procedure: 1. Reach steady state and confirm it. 2. Open the top-level window. 3. Force a template change. 4. Hold the window until dispatch has visibly resumed on the new template. 5. Lower the level, hold steady state again, and repeat the flush once more so the sequence can be compared against itself.
RDS-FLU-01.pass_fail: Pass: - The flush sequence is reconstructible from the capture, in order, with timings. - The two flushes agree. A sequence observed once is an anecdote. Fail: - Work in flight is lost in a way the daemon does not account for, and the discrepancy cannot be reconciled from the log. - A device does not resume dispatch after the flush.
RDS-FLU-01.metrics: Named before the run, not chosen after it. Across the flush window, at the top log level: every dispatch and every result, with timestamps, so work in flight at the moment of the template change can be accounted for. Elapsed time from the new template arriving to dispatch resuming. The count of results returned against the old template afterwards. Two flushes, so the sequence is measured against itself rather than described once.
RDS-FLU-01.comments: Our own flush path is the thing this case exists to specify and later to check. It is also the hardest case for the chain model in #57 to reproduce faithfully, which makes it the best test of whether that model is worth trusting.

MJ-HASH-01.title: Mujina hashing on boards the vendor powered
MJ-HASH-01.subtitle: ** not executed. GATED (G-HEAT), and blocked on the thermal interlock.** The first time our own code dispatches work to real silicon.
MJ-HASH-01.objective: Establish that Mujina can drive a powered BZM2 chain to produce verifiable work, and do it without relying on anything the vendor stack is still doing. Not "does it hash". Does it hash, safely, with every share externally verifiable and every watt accounted for.
MJ-HASH-01.requirements: - One RDS 2.0 unit, one hashboard, powered and calibrated by the vendor path. - The dispatch interlock, implemented and exercised against fault injection. - A pool and worker, with difficulty recorded, so shares are verifiable by something that is not us. - Metered wall power for the whole run, continuously, with no gaps. - An explicit go-ahead for the thermal load, recorded in the run.
MJ-HASH-01.procedure: 1. Bring one board up by the vendor path and let calibration settle. Record the operating point. 2. Hand over without dropping board power. 3. Confirm the interlock is armed and reporting a live die temperature before any work is dispatched. If it is not, the case aborts here, and that is a pass for the interlock. 4. Dispatch work at the recorded operating point. Hold for a stated duration after discarding a settling period. 5. Record submitted shares with their difficulty, metered power, die temperatures and fan state throughout. 6. Stop dispatching before stopping anything else, so the shutdown path is observed separately from the load being removed.
MJ-HASH-01.pass_fail: Pass: - Shares are accepted by the pool. The count and difficulty are the evidence; our own reported hash rate is not. - Die temperature stays within the ceiling for the whole run, and the interlock never has to act. If it does act, that is also a result, and a good one. - Power metering has no gaps. - The board returns to the vendor stack afterwards and powers on normally. Fail: - Any dispatch occurs before the interlock reports a live temperature. - Any board trips, or die temperature exceeds the ceiling. - A metering gap. A share count without the power that produced it is not a result, and the run is discarded rather than reported with a hole. - Shares rejected at a rate the pool's difficulty does not explain.
MJ-HASH-01.metrics: Named before the run, not chosen after it. Throughout: metered wall power without gaps, submitted shares with difficulty, die temperature per device, fan state, and the interlock's own view of whether telemetry is live. Elapsed time from dispatch starting to the first accepted share. Derived: joules per submitted share. Reported throughput is recorded but is not the measurement.
MJ-HASH-01.comments: The number this case exists to produce is joules per submitted share, which is the only efficiency figure that cannot be inflated by miscounting our own work. Reported throughput is self-reported; shares are not.

MJ-CMP-01.title: Vendor against Mujina, same board, same frequency, same hours
MJ-CMP-01.subtitle: ** not executed. GATED (G-HEAT).** Sustained mining. Needs an explicit go-ahead and a cool day.
MJ-CMP-01.objective: Establish whether Mujina reproduces the shipped stack's power and performance at a stated operating point, and by how much it beats or misses it — scored on **metered power against successfully submitted shares**, not on reported throughput.
MJ-CMP-01.requirements: - One RDS 2.0 unit, one hashboard. One board keeps the load near a kilowatt rather than three. - The same pool, worker and difficulty for every arm. A difficulty change between arms invalidates the comparison outright. - Metered wall power for the whole run, continuously, with no gaps. - Ambient and inlet temperature logged throughout, at the same cadence. - A stated frequency and voltage, identical in every arm, and **not** left to either stack's own calibration to choose — calibration is what MJ-CMP-01 is holding constant, not what it is measuring. - `rds-switch.sh` for the transitions, with each transition timestamped.
MJ-CMP-01.procedure: 1. Record the starting state: ambient, board serials, stored calibration, pool, worker, difficulty. 2. **Arm A1** — vendor stack at the stated point, two hours. Discard the first fifteen minutes as thermal settling; score the remainder. 3. Switch to Mujina. Record the transition timestamp and how long the board spent unpowered or idle, because that is the thermal discontinuity between arms. 4. **Arm B** — Mujina at the same stated point, two hours, same settling discard. 5. Switch back. 6. **Arm A2** — vendor stack again, two hours, same treatment. 7. Compute per arm: submitted shares, share difficulty, joules per share at the wall and at the rail, mean die temperature, mean ambient.
MJ-CMP-01.pass_fail: Pass: This case does not pass or fail Mujina. It produces a number and a confidence in it. The **run** is valid when: - Every arm ran its full window at the stated frequency and voltage, with no board dropping out. - Power metering has no gaps. - The two vendor arms agree within a tolerance argued from the ambient drift they measured — not a tolerance chosen to make them agree. Fail: - Any arm cut short, or any board trip. - A pool difficulty change mid-run. - The two bracketing arms disagreeing by more than the logged ambient drift can account for. That means something other than time changed between them, and the comparison is void until it is identified.
MJ-CMP-01.metrics: Named before the run, not chosen after it. Per arm, identically: metered wall power, submitted shares with difficulty, mean and spread of die temperature, mean ambient and inlet, and the settling period discarded. Derived per arm: joules per submitted share at both boundaries. Derived across arms: the difference between the two bracketing vendor arms, which is the ambient drift, and is the correction rather than a footnote.
MJ-CMP-01.comments: The headline number, and the only one that answers "is our stack worth running". Tonight's measurement says there is headroom to beat rather than merely match: the shipped calibration spends 95 J/TH at the margin to buy its last 13% of throughput, against a 29 J/TH average (#9). It also exercises the switch in both directions under load, which nothing else does.
MJ-CMP-01.configurations: One board, one stated operating point, three arms of two hours, fifteen minutes of settling discarded from each. Roughly six hours at about a kilowatt.
